lessons.title: Quantitative Data Sufficiency Basics
lessons.concept: Quantitative data sufficiency asks whether given statements provide enough information to answer a quantitative question (value, comparison, ratio, etc.). The focus is on sufficiency, not necessarily on performing full calculations. Evaluate each statement alone, then together if needed.
lessons.formula: Standard method: test Statement I alone; test Statement II alone; if neither sufficient, test I and II together. Avoid assuming unstated conditions (e.g., positive, integer) unless implied.
lessons.worked_example: Question: What is the value of a+b? I: a=5. II: b=3. I alone not sufficient, II alone not sufficient, together sufficient (a+b=8).
mistakes: Computing when not necessary instead of checking sufficiency
Assuming numbers are positive or integers without basis
Combining statements while evaluating them individually
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Sufficiency in Value and Comparison Questions
lessons.concept: For value questions, a statement is sufficient if it yields a unique value. For comparison/yes-no questions (e.g., Is x > y?), a statement is sufficient if it gives a definite answer (always yes or always no). If multiple outcomes are possible, it is not sufficient.
lessons.formula: Unique value => sufficient. Definite yes/no => sufficient. Multiple possible answers => not sufficient.
lessons.worked_example: Question: Is x > 0? I: x = -2 gives definite No, so I alone is sufficient. II: x^2 = 4 gives x=2 or -2, so II alone not sufficient.
mistakes: Thinking a range is sufficient for a unique-value question
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Common Quantitative Traps
lessons.concept: Common traps include missing multiple solutions (quadratics), sign ambiguity, assuming non-zero denominators or distinct values, and ignoring that together statements may still be insufficient. Always verify whether the information uniquely determines the answer.
lessons.formula: Check for: multiple roots, positive/negative cases, zero cases, integer/non-integer cases as relevant.
lessons.worked_example: Question: What is x? I: x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 gives x=2 or 3 (not sufficient). II: x > 2 gives many values (not sufficient). Together x=3 (sufficient).
mistakes: Taking only one root of a quadratic
Ignoring constraints implied by combining statements correctly
Assuming variables are integers unless stated

practice.question: Question: What is the value of x? I: x + 4 = 9. II: x > 0. Which is sufficient?
practice.explanation: Statement I gives x = 5 uniquely, so it is sufficient. Statement II alone allows many values.

practice.question: Question: What is area of a circle? I: Radius is 7 cm. II: Diameter is 14 cm. Which is correct?

options.A: I alone sufficient, II alone not
options.B: II alone sufficient, I alone not

practice.explanation: Area = πr^2 and diameter gives radius (r=d/2). Either statement alone determines the circle size and area.

questions.question: Question: What is the perimeter of square S? I: Side of S is 6 cm. II: Area of S is 36 cm^2. Which is correct?

options.A: I alone sufficient, II alone not
options.B: II alone sufficient, I alone not

questions.explanation: From I, perimeter = 4*6 = 24 cm. From II, side = sqrt(36)=6 cm (length positive), perimeter = 24 cm. Each alone sufficient.
